'''''Amaryllis belladonna''''',<ref>{{cite book |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/358312#page/305/mode/1up |last=Linnaeus |first=Carl |year=1753 |title=Species Plantarum |volume=1 |page=293 |via=Biodiversity Heritage Library}}</ref> the '''Jersey lily''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=17 October 2014 }}</ref> '''belladonna-lily''', '''naked-lady-lily''',{{sfn|RHS|2015}} or '''March lily''',{{sfn|Phipps|2011}} is a plant species native to [[Cape Province]] in South Africa but widely cultivated as an ornamental. It is reportedly [[Naturalisation (biology)|naturalized]] in many places: [[Corsica]], Portugal, the [[Azores]], [[Madeira]], the [[Canary Islands]], the [[Scilly Isles]] of Great Britain, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, [[Ascension Island]], Australia, New Zealand, Mexico, Cuba, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, Chile, California, Texas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Michigan, Indiana and the [[Juan Fernández Islands]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/namedetail.do?name_id=298570 |work=Kew World Checklist of Selected Plant Families |title=Amaryllis belladonna}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://bonap.net/MapGallery/County/Amaryllis%20belladonna.png |title=Amaryllis Belladona distribution map |publisher=Biota of North America Project}}</ref>

== Description ==
[[Perennial]] [[bulbous]] [[geophyte]] with one to two erect solid stems which appear in late summer. The [[inflorescence]] bears 2–12 showy fragrant funnel-shaped flowers on a 'naked' (leafless) stem, which gives it the common name of naked-lady-lily. The pink flowers which may be up to {{Convert abbreviated|10|cm}} in length, appear in the autumn before the leaves ([[hysteranthy]]) which are narrow and strap shaped.{{sfn|RHS|2015}}{{sfn|Phipps|2011}}

== Taxonomy and etymology ==
''Amaryllis belladonna'' is one of the two species in the genus ''[[Amaryllis]]'' as currently [[Circumscription (taxonomy)|circumscribed]].<ref name="WCSP_Amaryllis">{{cite web |title=Search for ''Amaryllis'' |work=[[World Checklist of Selected Plant Families]] |publisher=[[Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]] |url=http://apps.kew.org/wcsp/qsearch.do?plantName=Amaryllis |access-date=1 February 2015}}</ref>

The [[Binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''belladonna'' is derived from the Italian ''bella donna'', which means beautiful lady.<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NJ6PyhVuecwC |title=The Names of Plants |first=David |last=Gledhill |edition=4th |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-86645-3 |year=2008 |page=68}}</ref>

== Habitat ==
''Amaryllis belladonna'' is found in South Africa, where the plants are found growing among rocks.{{sfn|Phipps|2011}}

== Ecology ==
Leaves of ''A. belladonna'' begin growing in early spring, or during late autumn. They last for a few weeks to a few months until they wither away, and a flower stalk will begin growing. When found in the wild, ''Amaryllis belladonna'' is pollinated by [[Sphingidae|hawk moths]] and [[Carpenter bee|carpenter bees]]. The flower has a long-tubed, pale [[perianth]], which fully expands at night. This flower will then release a sweet fragrance, that contains acyclic terpenoid [[Alcohol (chemistry)|alcohol]], [[linalool]] and abundant [[nectar]], that attracts pollinators to it.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Manning |first1=J. C. |last2=Snijman |first2=D. |date=1 July 2002 |title=Hawkmoth-pollination in ''Crinum variabile'' (Amaryllidaceae) and the biogeography of sphingophily in southern African Amaryllidaceae |journal=South African Journal of Botany |language=en |volume=68 |issue=2 |pages=212–216 |doi=10.1016/S0254-6299(15)30422-1 |doi-access=free}}</ref> ''A. belladonna'' seeds are soft and fleshy, and appear white or pinkish. They are dispersed through [[wind dispersal]] during the winter time. This is to coincide with the first winter rain during March, and April. Seeds will germinate in as early as two weeks, but will not develop into a fully flowering plant until three to six years later.{{citation needed|date=February 2021}}

All parts of the ''A. belladonna'' plant are toxic and contain several different alkaloids, such as [[lycorine]], [[pancracine]] and [[Amaryllidinae|amaryllidine]]. This can cause vomiting and diarrhea in humans. In wildlife these toxins will affect [[Grazing (behaviour)|grazing]] species, and will cause drooling, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal distress, lethargy, and heart or renal failure. Deer will avoid eating this plant, possibly due to an evolutionary relationship.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Is Amaryllis Belladonna Toxic? |url=https://www.gardenguides.com/12427955-is-amaryllis-belladonna-toxic.html |access-date=19 February 2021 |website=Garden Guides |language=en}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
The bulbs are best planted just below the surface of the soil, with the neck of the bulb level with the surface. In colder climates [[mulching]] or lifting and [[overwintering]] is required. The bulbs may be propagated from [[offset (botany)|offset]]s. Amaryllis bulbs require little watering and are drought tolerant.{{sfn|Phipps|2011}} This plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{sfn|RHS|2015}}

== Medicinal properties ==
Several compounds have been found in ''A. belladonna'' bulbs, including, 1,4-dihydroxy-3-methoxy powellan, which is an [[alkaloid]]. It has been observed that alkaloids in this plants bulb have properties to fight against [[malaria]] caused by ''[[Plasmodium falciparum|P. falciparum]].''<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cho |first1=Namki |last2=Du |first2=Yongle |last3=Valenciano |first3=Ana Lisa |last4=Fernández-Murga |first4=Maria L. |last5=Goetz |first5=Michael |last6=Clement |first6=Jason |last7=Cassera |first7=Maria B. |last8=Kingston |first8=David G. I. |date=1 January 2018 |title=Antiplasmodial alkaloids from bulbs of ''Amaryllis belladonna'' Steud. |url= |journal=Bioorganic & Medicinal Chemistry Letters |language=en |volume=28 |issue=1 |pages=40–42 |doi=10.1016/j.bmcl.2017.11.021 |pmid=29162457 |pmc=5753767}}</ref>
